summary: Rawlinson worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and history and archaeology. Educated at Great Ealing School and Middlesex University, he held posts with the East India Company (~1827–1858), the Foreign Office, and the Royal Geographical Society (~1871–1876).

Shiu specializes in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He completed his PhD at the University of Toronto in 2006, having studied under Shek-wing Tam, Leonard C. D. C. Priestley, David Waterhouse, and Willard Gurdon Oxtoby.
Olcott worked in religious and Buddhist studies. He studied at Columbia University (~1847–1849) and founded the Theosophical Society in 1875.
Jarrett was active in history, archaeology, and other fields. He served as Secretary and Member of the Board of Examiners at Fort William (~1870–1894), where he succeeded Heinrich Blochmann.

Colebrooke worked in Indology and studied under Citrapati. He served with the East India Company (~1782–1814), held a professorship at Fort William College (1782–1814), and served as president of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland (~1823–1837).

Tolman was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Yale, Peabody College, and the universities of Nashville, Hobart, and Louisville, later holding posts at Yale, Wisconsin-Madison, UNC-Chapel Hill, and Vanderbilt (1894–1923).

Franke worked in sinology, history, and archaeology, studying at Bonn, Humboldt University, and Cologne under Erich Haenisch and Erich Hauer. He was a professor at the University of Munich (1952–1979) and president of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities (~1980–1985).
Risley worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He was educated at Winchester College (~1863–1869) and New College, Oxford (~1869–1873).

Härtel was an Indologist and archaeologist. After studying at Halle and Göttingen under Ernst Waldschmidt, he served at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin (~1953–1986), directed the Museum of Asian Art (1963–1986), and held professorships at the Free University and Humboldt University.
Randle worked in Indology and philosophy. He served as professor of philosophy at Sampurnanand Sanskrit University (~1910–1927) and as librarian at the India Office and its Library (~1933–1949).

Günther specialized in Buddhist studies, tibetology, and philosophy, earning doctorates at Munich and Vienna under Wilhelm Geiger and Wilhelm Havers. He held posts at Lucknow, Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, and the University of Saskatchewan, where he headed Far Eastern Studies (1964–1984).

Smyth worked in linguistics, history, and archaeology, studying at Swarthmore, Harvard, Leipzig, and Göttingen under Hermann Sauppe. He held academic posts at Williams College, Bryn Mawr (1887–1901), and Harvard University (from 1901).
Kellgren was a scholar in linguistics and Indology. He studied under Hermann Brockhaus, Eugène Burnouf, and Philippe-Édouard Foucaux, and held a post at the University of Helsinki (~1849–1856).
Wirth worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Utrecht University (~1904–1908), held a post at the University of Bern (~1909–1914), and founded the Ahnenerbe.

Beckh worked in Indology, tibetology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Kiel University and Humboldt University of Berlin, later working at the Prussian State Library (~1908–1921) and as a Privatdozent at Humboldt University (~1912–1921).
Berger specialized in Indology and linguistics. He studied under Helmut Hoffmann (~1949–1957) and took up a post at Heidelberg University in 1965.
Beythan was a scholar in linguistics and Indology who studied under traditional teachers Ramasami Aiyar and Radscha Pillai.

Bonitz worked in philosophy and linguistics, having studied at Leipzig University and Humboldt University of Berlin. He held posts at the University of Vienna (~1849–1867) and the Prussian Ministry of Spiritual, Educational and Medical Affairs (~1875–1888).

Brockhaus specialized in Indology and linguistics, studying at Leipzig, Göttingen, and Bonn under August Wilhelm Schlegel. He held professorships at the University of Jena (1839) and Leipzig University (~1848–1877), where he also served as rector (1872–1873).

Brunnhofer was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Bonn, Berlin, and Zurich under Albrecht Weber. His career included posts at Kuldīga Gymnasium, Oxford, Saint Petersburg State University, and the University of Bern (1901–1914).
